item.title: Cholinergic blockade reveals a role for human hippocampal theta in memory encoding but not retrieval.
item.description:
eLife
Cholinergic dysfunction is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease and other memory disorders. Yet, the neurophysiological mechanisms linking cholinergic signaling to memory remain poorly understood. In this study, we administered scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, to neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes as they performed an associative recognition memory task. When scopolamine was present at encoding, we observed disruptions to hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2-4 Hz), with selective impairments to recollection-based memory. However, when scopolamine was present during retrieval alone, we observed disruptions to slow theta without impaired memory performance. These disruptions included dose-dependent reductions in theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding-retrieval pattern reinstatement. Together, our results challenge the notion that theta oscillations are necessary for memory retrieval, and instead suggest that theta universally reflects an encoding-related neural state. These findings motivate updates to current models of acetylcholine's role in memory and may inform future therapies targeting rhythmic biomarkers of memory dysfunction.

item.title: Learning to Navigate a Changing World: From Brain Systems to Novel Algorithms.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Natural organisms navigate a world in constant flux and are frequently confronted with sensory ambiguity and shifting goals. While biological systems can adapt rapidly to navigate in novel and nonstationary environments, this challenge remains a significant hurdle for artificial intelligence. In this review, we examine recent progress in understanding neurobiological systems that allow for adaptive, efficient spatial and abstract navigation in dynamic environments and how these observations have informed new developments for the same behavior in machines. We highlight how predictive learning serves as a unifying framework to describe the organization of neural activity across distributed systems for navigation, including the hippocampal formation, parietal cortex, and higher-order associative structures. Specifically, we explore how such neurobiological systems encode expected future states, dynamic target trajectories, action plans, and internal behavioral strategies. Finally, we contrast the diffuse, inefficient exploration of canonical artificial agents with the structured, efficient control policies for goal-directed navigation observed in natural organisms. By grounding learning in the interplay between action, prediction, and natural behavioral statistics, navigation provides a roadmap for building resilient, neurobiologically inspired continual learning in artificial agents.

item.title: Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning.Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

item.title: Capturing Habits in Humans: Neural Circuitry, Computations, and Clinical Mechanisms.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Habits allow repeated behaviors to be executed efficiently, but habitual control can contribute to maladaptive inflexibility when it dominates despite changing goals or consequences. This review examines recent advances in understanding habitual control across neural circuits, computation, clinical phenotypes, and measurement. We first consider dorsomedial striatal mechanisms that support action-outcome learning and flexible goal-directed behavior and how chronic stress can alter striatal inputs to bias learning toward habitual control. Progress on what computational reinforcement-learning accounts for arbitration between goal-directed and habitual systems is described along prefrontal mechanisms guiding model-based control, action perseveration, and compulsivity in obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). A wider behavioral spectrum beyond action initiation is provided, reviewing emerging work on habitual inhibition and frontostriatal circuit dynamics of avoidance in OCD. Recent laboratory paradigms aim to reveal habit formation more sensitively than traditional outcome-devaluation paradigms, whereas real-world digital approaches use smartphones, wearables, and intensive longitudinal measurement to track habit formation and expression in everyday life. Integrating these approaches can help link habits to physiology, symptoms and neural circuits across laboratory to real-world and clinical contexts.

item.title: Janus in Thermosensation: The Dual Interoceptive-Exteroceptive Nature of Thermal Signals in Body Ownership.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Thermosensation has traditionally been studied for its essential role in survival, enabling detection of environmental thermal stimuli and the maintenance of thermal homeostasis. Interestingly, unlike most sensory systems, thermosensation provides information about both the external world and the body's internal physiological state. In this review, we conceptualize these two dimensions as exteroceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the thermal properties of external objects and the environment, and interoceptive thermosensation, which conveys information about the body's thermal state. Growing evidence suggests that this dual nature serves functions that extend beyond survival and homeostasis. Alterations in both thermal perception and thermoregulation have been associated with changes in body ownership, the experience that one's body belongs to oneself, while manipulations of thermal signals can influence ownership itself. Here, we review the physiological and neural bases of exteroceptive and interoceptive thermosensation, from peripheral encoding to central processing, and examine their relationship with body ownership in healthy and clinical populations. We discuss evidence suggesting partially distinct yet potentially convergent neural substrates for these two dimensions of thermosensation, highlighting the insular cortex and its broader connectivity network as a candidate through which thermal information may sustain body ownership. Finally, we consider how emerging neurotechnologies offer new opportunities to investigate the contribution of thermosensation to body ownership while also opening novel avenues for neurorehabilitation. We propose that thermosensation represents an underexplored contributor to body ownership, opening new avenues for future research on how bodily and environmental thermal signals are integrated to support the sense of self.

item.title: Cross-Species Approaches to Understanding Human Cognition.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Recent methodological advances including high-density intracranial recordings and population-level analytical frameworks enable deeper and more direct integration between animal models and human neuroscience. As a result, there is an increasing need for standardized behavioral paradigms and circuit-level analyses that can be used in both animals and humans. Cross-species approaches provide crucial foundations for treating neurological and psychiatric disorders. Parallel experiments validate therapeutic targets and enable development of mechanistically grounded behavioral biomarkers for early disease detection. Here, we provide a brief review of recent findings that have direct implications for attention deficits, memory impairments, and decision-making dysfunctions. By linking mechanism to behavior, these approaches guide targeted interventions and effective clinical translation. While challenges remain, these integrated approaches are advancing our understanding of the mechanistic foundation of human cognition.

item.title: Revisiting Post-stimulus Theta Activity: Evidence for a Broadband Rather Than Narrowband Spectral Origin.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The aperiodic, 1/f -like component of electrophysiological activity is increasingly recognized as a meaningful feature of neural function rather than background noise. Meanwhile, many EEG studies interpret transient post-stimulus changes in oscillatory power as signatures of attention, salience, or cognitive control. Such interpretations typically depend on baseline normalization, which assumes aperiodic activity remains stable from pre- to post-stimulus periods. Using high-density EEG from typically developing children, we tested this assumption across two paradigms: an audiovisual simple reaction-time task (n = 36, 19 males and 17 females) and a visual oddball task (n = 38, 20 males and 18 females). In each, conventional spectral analyses were compared with analyses that explicitly modeled and removed aperiodic activity in both windows. Across tasks, stimulus onset produced robust increases in aperiodic exponent and offset, indicating systematic 1/f changes. In the audiovisual task these were modality specific, with central, parieto-occipital, or combined topographies by stimulus type. They diminished but persisted after event-related potential removal, suggesting they were not fully explained by phase-locked activity. Critically, once aperiodic activity was accounted for, the apparent theta increase was largely abolished in both tasks, including the canonical fronto-central enhancement to infrequent targets. The conventional method also overestimated beta desynchronization, especially in the induced signal, indicating a spurious consequence of spectral slope steepening. In contrast, alpha desynchronization remained robust and was enhanced, reflecting genuine suppression. Together, these findings suggest many conventional time-frequency effects, particularly apparent theta synchronization, may reflect stimulus-driven aperiodic changes rather than robust narrowband changes, challenging core assumptions of these analyses.

item.title: NeuroAI's Next Steps: Balancing Computation and Embodiment.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Deep neural networks trained at scale now predict neural activity across sensory cortices, raising a question that divides neuroscience: does the convergence between artificial and biological representations constitute understanding, or does understanding require models of biological processes grounded in the embodied, evolved character of natural intelligence? In this Dual Perspectives article, Bing Brunton and Patrick Mineault articulate two research programs-Process and Convergence-to engage this question about the future of NeuroAI research. The conversation is organized around four questions that probe what scaled model-brain alignment reveals, what the brain is coupled to and evolved to do, what success beyond the lab looks like, and where the field should invest over the coming decade. Their exchanges reveal the distance between the two programs to be primarily about the level of analysis and priorities for what to build next. The conversation converges on shared ground: measure broadly, then distill to causal principles.

item.title: Embodied Computation: How Does Embodiment Impact Sensorimotor and Cognitive Processing?
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Animals act on the world through a physical body and continually adjust behavior in response to the sensory feedback their actions produce. This closed loop between brain, body, and environment is central to motor control, but its role in other neural computations remains less clear. This review focuses on embodied computation: how the physical body shapes neural activity and behavior across functions ranging from motor control to cognitive processes. We examine the impact of embodiment in several domains, including compositional reuse, intrinsic motivation, metabolic costs, and connectome-constrained computation, with the broader aim of asking when the body can be abstracted away and when it is essential for explaining what the brain computes.

item.title: Hidden Vision and Beyond: Multiscale Foundations of Thalamic Organization.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The subcortical visual system is traditionally described through a small number of canonical pathways, with the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) viewed primarily as a first-order relay to primary visual cortex and additional routes through the superior colliculus, pulvinar and koniocellular LGN considered secondary or residual. Here, we review recent evidence across species, methods, and scales that challenge this framework and suggest that the visual thalamus is an active, dynamically regulated component of visual processing. We first consider primary and nonprimary visual pathways, showing how thalamic inputs shape cortical responses through the timing, spatial arrangement, synaptic organization, laminar targeting, and circuit-level integration of feedforward signals. We then reconsider the "first-order" status of LGN itself, reviewing evidence that nonretinal subcortical inputs, local inhibition, and corticothalamic feedback can alter LGN responses and the signals routed onward to cortex. This shifts the view of LGN from a passive relay supplying a dynamic cortex to a dynamically regulated node in its own right. Next, we review advances in higher-order thalamic organization, highlighting structured thalamocortical connectivity, network-level coordination, and state-dependent dynamics. Finally, we consider how thalamic functions change in the injured brain, where emerging models disentangle acute effects of damage from chronic compensation to reveal how surviving thalamic and downstream pathways may be remodeled, reweighted, or recruited to support residual visual function and recovery. Together, these findings support a multiscale view of the thalamus as a collection of specialized, adaptive nuclei embedded within distributed cortico-subcortical networks, with implications for perception, cognition, sensory disorders, and rehabilitation.

item.title: Six Challenges for a Mechanistic Science of Human Interoception.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Human interoception has become a major focus of systems, cognitive, and clinical neuroscience. Work across the past decade has shown that signals originating within the body shape perception, emotion, cognition, behavior, and health. Despite rapid methodological and conceptual progress, which substantially expanded our understanding of how bodily signals are processed and represented, much of the field remains constrained by descriptive methods. As these approaches passively assess bodily signals or subjective awareness, they have limited ability to establish causal mechanisms or translate interoceptive findings into clinically informative frameworks. Here, we identify six challenges and corresponding methodological directions for advancing human interoception research: strengthening integration of animal and human models, developing causal perturbation paradigms, capturing interoception in ecologically valid contexts, standardizing multidimensional measurement across bodily systems, adjudicating between computational accounts, and translating mechanistic insights into clinically informative models of health and disease. These challenges are best understood as linked requirements for moving interoception research from relevance to mechanism. Together, they highlight the need to move beyond predominantly static, passive, and single-modality approaches toward studies that can test how internal bodily signals relate to neural activity, behavior, and health.

item.title: Parallel Claustral Networks for Behavioral Control in Health and Disease.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The claustrum is among the most highly interconnected structures in the mammalian brain, with reciprocal projections spanning the cortical mantle and a growing roster of functions that range from sleep regulation to attentional control. Here we review current understanding of claustral circuit organization and function, synthesizing findings from anatomical, physiological, computational, and behavioral studies. We argue that a unifying logic underlies the apparent diversity of claustral functions: the claustrum operates through projection-defined subnetworks whose input selectivity, output targets, and local circuit interactions collectively determine their functional contribution and whose impact on cortical targets varies with arousal and ongoing brain state. Corticoclaustral connectivity is organized into matched input-output modules, local inhibitory circuits confer spatial filtering properties that amplify strong cortical signals while suppressing weaker ones and claustral output populations differ in their laminar targets, postsynaptic cell-type preferences, and molecular properties, producing diverse and context-dependent effects on cortical dynamics. These circuit properties translate into claustral regulation of cortical population dynamics across multiple timescales, from the moment-to-moment coordination of brain states to the consolidation of frontal control strategies. In pain and addiction, specific claustral projection populations are selectively dysregulated, and distinct subnetworks exert opposing influences on nociceptive sensitivity and drug-related behavior according to their cortical targets. Together, these findings position the claustrum as a modular subcortical hub for the selective regulation of distributed cortical networks and identify it as a candidate therapeutic target for disorders characterized by dysregulated cortical network activity, including chronic pain, addiction, and impulsivity.

item.title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations during Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgments and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N = 80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision process.

item.title: Emotional Content Enhances Attentional Tracking of Conversations through Context-Sensitive Modulation of Auditory-Language Networks.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Engagement in conversation often requires continuous monitoring of relevant speech in a continuously evolving auditory environment. Emotional salience of semantic content may influence this process, but its role in attentional tracking of continuous speech remains unclear. We address this question using an audiovisual "cocktail-party" paradigm combined with source-localized magnetoencephalography and encoding-decoding analyses. Participants (18 females, 14 males) selectively attended to one dialogue while ignoring a concurrent distractor dialogue, with both emotional salience and semantic coherence of the conversations manipulated independently. Decoding analyses revealed that negatively valenced, high-arousal, and socially relevant semantic content strengthened neural speech tracking, but only for attended dialogues. This effect depended on semantic structure, emerging earlier in semantically coherent than incoherent dialogues. Encoding analyses further showed latency- and region-specific effects across temporal, parietal, and frontal cortical regions. Emotional salience and coherence jointly modulated midlatency (100-250 ms) responses, whereas late-latency (270-450 ms) responses were driven primarily by emotional salience. These findings demonstrate that emotional meaning enhances neural prioritization of attended speech and semantic coherence shapes the temporal dynamics of this enhancement. Together, these results indicate context-sensitive emotional modulation of auditory-language processing during selective listening of continuous speech.

item.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region's future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain's memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

item.title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces-a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Functional brain signatures of successful cognitive aging.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Cognitive aging trajectories vary markedly. While many older adults experience gradual decline in memory and executive function, some maintain high cognitive performance well into advanced age. Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying this variability carries important implications for early detection of unfavorable aging trajectories and the development of interventions. Here, we review functional brain signatures associated with successful cognitive aging in humans, integrating evidence from functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography within a unified conceptual framework of brain maintenance and compensation. Across both modalities, evidence increasingly links successful cognitive aging to the preservation of youth-like neural dynamics, while the contribution of compensatory neural recruitment remains empirically contested and methodologically difficult to establish.

item.title: Decoupling language and emotion in the bilingual brain.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
In a recent article, Davydova et al. showed that affect labeling fails in a second, less-proficient language due to the amygdala-ventrolateral prefrontal cortex functional connectivity. This subcortical decoupling also explains the emotional blunting that bilinguals report when using their less-proficient language.

item.title: Spontaneously emerging patterns show category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns beyond human visual cortex.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In the absence of any task, spontaneous brain activity exhibits patterns that resemble those evoked by natural stimuli and behaviors. This raises the possibility that resting-state activity patterns may relate to maintenance and consolidation of behaviorally relevant information states. Using functional MRI (fMRI) data from 100 healthy adults in the Human Connectome Project, we investigated whether neural signals evoked by specific visual stimuli (body parts, faces, places, tools) show similarity to resting-state activity across non-canonical visual areas, i.e., motor and association cortices. Participants underwent a working memory task and resting-state scanning. We analyzed multivoxel pattern similarity between task-evoked activations and spontaneous activity in bilateral hand motor regions and attention-related networks. Spatial correlations between task-evoked multivoxel patterns for each visual category and frame-by-frame resting-state signals were computed, with the upper 90% distribution percentile (U90) as a similarity metric. We found that resting-state patterns in the left hemisphere hand motor region showed significantly higher similarity to tool-evoked patterns than place-evoked patterns, consistent with the interpretation that tools recruit motor affordances and hand‑object associations in motor cortex. In the bilateral dorsal attention network, resting-task similarity for non-face evoked patterns significantly exceeded that for faces. Moreover, effects localized to posterior dorsal attention network, aligning with the dorsal visual pathway's role in spatial-action coding of behaviorally relevant objects. These results suggest that resting-state activity in non-visual cortices shows category-biased similarity to task-evoked visual patterns, consistent with the view that spontaneous neural dynamics preferentially reactivate ecologically salient stimuli.

item.title: Transdiagnostic variation in age-related patterns of rich-club organization across neurodevelopmental and related mental health conditions.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Rich-club organization is a topographical property of functional brain networks where highly connected regions are more densely interconnected. The rich-club has been shown to be vital for supporting cognitive functioning, and differences have been associated with a wide range of mental health and developmental conditions. This type of organization undergoes complex changes across development, and we have previously shown that males and females have strikingly distinct age-related changes. While disruptions in its development have been related to neurodevelopmental conditions and related mental health conditions such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), the diagnostic- and sex-specific age-related patterns remain unexplored. These conditions also have heterogeneous and overlapping neurobiology and phenotype, and thus transdiagnostic approaches may be most suitable for addressing the complexities. Here, we combine the temporal advantages of magnetoencephalography (MEG) with a data-driven, transdiagnostic approach to parse the heterogeneity of age-related variation in rich-club organization in 386 neurodivergent (116 ADHD, 231 autism, 39 OCD) and 231 neurotypical children and youth, stratified by biological sex. In males and females, subgroups with distinct age-related patterns of rich-club organization did not align cleanly with the diagnostic categories. These patterns were frequency specific, separating the female subgroups in the alpha and gamma bands and the male subgroups in the theta, alpha, beta, and high gamma bands. While the female subgroups differed in their proportions of autistic and neurotypical individuals, all diagnostic categories were represented across the subgroups. The female subgroups also differed in intelligence, while the male subgroups differed in hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms. Together, our findings indicate that frequency-specific, age-related variation in rich-club organization is largely shared across neurotypical and neurodivergent children and youth, rather than delineating diagnostic categories, and highlight the importance of considering sex when studying the biological constructs underlying neurodivergence.

item.title: Neural Connectome Mapping of Chronotype in Young Adults: Associations with Neurotransmitter Profiles and Longitudinal Self-Control.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Chronotype is associated with self-regulation, but its functional connectivity correlates, neurotransmitter correspondence, and longitudinal associations with self-control remain unclear. We applied connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) in a longitudinal cohort to identify resting-state connectivity features associated with chronotype. Cross-validated predictions showed a small correlation with reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ) scores in the discovery set (n = 816, r = 0.118, pperm = 0.007). A similar association was observed in validation set 1, a baseline hold-out sample from the same cohort (n = 681, r = 0.125, pperm < 0.001). Longitudinal evaluation used validation set 2, comprising two-year follow-up data from a subset of participants in validation set 1 (n = 594, r = 0.134, pperm < 0.001), providing a within-cohort assessment of whether the association was stable over time. Node-importance maps showed spatial correspondence with neurotransmitter maps. Both connectivity sets shared GABA-A and VAChT associations, with relatively receptor-weighted and transporter-weighted profiles in the positive and negative sets, respectively. In participants with complete two-wave data (n = 563), cross-lagged panel models indicated that baseline self-control was prospectively associated with higher positive-set strength (β = 0.256, p < 0.001) and lower negative-set strength (β = -0.228, p < 0.001); reverse paths were not significant. These findings provide evidence for chronotype-related functional connectivity features and their associations with neurotransmitter distributions and self-control in young adults. The validation and longitudinal evidence is limited to a single-site cohort, and cross-cohort generalizability remains to be established.

item.title: Age-related reversal in the behavioral relevance of theta-alpha coupling during conflict processing.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Cognitive aging is often characterized by slower responses during conflict processing, but the oscillatory coordination underlying this change remains poorly understood. We examined whether cross-frequency phase synchronization between theta and alpha activity is related to response conflict processing and whether its behavioral relevance changes across adulthood. N = 117 healthy adults aged 32-84 years performed a flanker task while an EEG was recorded. Theta-alpha phase-phase coupling was quantified as phase-locking value (PLV) across task-relevant time windows; time-frequency and source-level analyses characterized the underlying dynamics. Incongruent trials produced robust behavioral conflict, with lower accuracy and slower responses than congruent trials. Theta-alpha coupling showed a pronounced 1:1 structure across conditions, and was selectively stronger during incongruent trials. Time-frequency and source-level analysis provided complementary evidence of frontocentral theta engagement and alpha modulation in posterior and sensorimotor regions. Theta-alpha PLV at FCz during the target-processing window declined with age in incongruent trials, and its association with reaction time varied with age in the incongruent-trial analysis. Stronger coupling was associated with faster responses at younger ages, whereas the same coupling was associated with slower responses at older ages. A direct comparison did not establish that this age-dependent association differed between congruent and incongruent trials. These findings suggest that theta-alpha coupling is sensitive to response conflict and may contribute to the coordination of control-related and gating-related processes. Its age-related decline and changing association with response speed highlight the relevance of cross-frequency coordination for understanding cognitive aging.

item.title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

item.title: Subliminal beauty engages the brain's valuation circuits.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Neuroeconomic models propose that the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are key regions for computing subjective value (SV) signals that guide choice. However, the role of conscious awareness in this process remains debated. Here we examined whether SV can be automatically computed in these regions without conscious awareness. In an fMRI experiment, human participants (24 females, 5 males) viewed faces that varied in attractiveness under three conditions: (i) suppressed from awareness via continuous flash suppression (CFS), (ii) clearly visible without suppression, or (iii) absent (background only) with CFS. Participants reported trial-wise facial identity (objective) and visibility (subjective) measures of facial awareness. In a post-fMRI session, they rated the attractiveness of each face as a measure of SV. When faces were seen, task performance (d') exceeded chance and responses were faster than in absent trials. When faces were unseen, performance was at chance but responses were slower than absent trials. Neurally, seen and unseen faces elicited greater neural signal than absent trials and showed similar neural patterns in the fusiform face area (FFA). Critically, neural signal in vmPFC correlated with SV for both seen and unseen faces, with similar neural patterns. In aVS, SV-related signal was only observed for unseen faces. Furthermore, mean face-related signal in FFA correlated with SV-related signals in aVS and vmPFC for unseen faces. These findings demonstrate that SV can be automatically computed in aVS and vmPFC without conscious awareness, suggesting a neural pathway by which subliminal information can influence value-based choice.Significance statement A central question in consciousness research and decision neuroscience is whether the brain's valuation circuitry - particularly the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) - can compute subjective value automatically without conscious awareness. This question is important because prevailing accounts often assume that cognitive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex require conscious awareness of task-relevant information. Using continuous flash suppression and neuroimaging, we found that faces reported unseen nevertheless evoked value-related signals in aVS and vmPFC that scaled with subjective attractiveness ratings. These findings demonstrate that subjective value can be computed automatically from social information in the absence of conscious awareness.

item.title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x106 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x104 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x104 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates.Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

item.title: Broadband gamma-band EEG changes during magnetophosphene-inducing 20 Hz magnetic field stimulation.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Magnetophosphenes are visual percepts induced by extremely low-frequency magnetic fields (ELF-MF; <300 Hz), yet the EEG expression of suprathreshold magnetophosphene-inducing stimulation remains poorly characterized and is not reliably captured by classical low-frequency markers. We tested whether suprathreshold 20 Hz tAMS is accompanied by broadband high-frequency EEG changes rather than focal oscillatory effects. EEG was recorded in N=13 healthy volunteers during 20 Hz sinusoidal magnetic-field exposure delivered using transcranial alternating magnetic stimulation (tAMS) in a global-head configuration. Three conditions were analyzed: no exposure (0 mT), subthreshold (5 mT), and suprathreshold (50 mT). Gamma-band EEG power (30-80 Hz) was quantified using complementary spectral approaches, including aperiodic-adjusted gamma power. Perception reports sharply dissociated the three conditions, with frequent perception at 50 mT only. Suprathreshold stimulation was associated with spatially distributed increases in gamma-band EEG power over frontal and occipito-parietal electrodes. The differences remained partly detectable in complementary analyses using two local aperiodic-adjustment methods and did not exhibit a consistent narrowband peak, a pattern consistent with broadband high-frequency changes. No focal power change over primary occipital electrodes remained significant after Bonferroni correction. These findings identify a spatially distributed broadband high-frequency scalp EEG effect associated with the suprathreshold 50 mT condition, with the main spatial pattern strongly preserved after ICA-based removal of components classified as ocular or muscular. The effect therefore characterizes the coupled suprathreshold stimulation-perception condition; its perception specificity and physiological source remain unresolved.

item.title: Load-dependent brain network reconfiguration deficits in childhood ADHD revealed by source-space MEG and Graph Transformer modeling.
item.description:
Developmental cognitive neuroscience
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is clinically heterogeneous, motivating biomarkers that capture how brain networks reorganize under cognitive demand. We studied 122 children aged 8-12 years (61 with ADHD and 61 controls) during a visually cued attention/inhibition paradigm spanning three operationalized composite demand levels in whole-head MEG; structural MRI supported anatomical source modeling, and 34 children with ADHD completed approximately 6 months of follow-up. After denoising, head-motion compensation, ICA-based artifact removal, dSPM source reconstruction, and Morlet wavelet decomposition, we extracted source time series from 68 DKT cortical regions, quantified dynamic connectivity with PLV, wPLI, AEC, and MI, derived graph-theoretic and hidden Markov model features, and trained a spatiotemporal Graph Transformer. Behavioral group differences increased with cognitive demand, with high-load accuracy showing a large effect size (d=1.71). Relative to controls, children with ADHD showed weaker frontoparietal θ coupling, stronger default-mode α coupling, reduced occupancy of frontoparietal-dominant states, greater default-mode state persistence, lower global efficiency, higher modularity, and smaller gains in network flexibility; frontoparietal flexibility showed the strongest association with inattentive symptoms (rs =-0.78). Under participant-level nested cross-validation, the Graph Transformer achieved 94.3% accuracy for three-class cognitive-demand classification (AUC = 0.981) and 96.7% accuracy for ADHD diagnosis (AUC = 0.991). Secondary presentation analyses reached 83.6% accuracy (95% CI: 73.8%-91.8%), and higher baseline frontoparietal flexibility in the follow-up subset was associated with subsequent medication response (OR = 8.49, 95% CI: 2.31-31.2). In an independent task-matched MEG cohort (n=45), zero-shot ADHD diagnostic accuracy was 90.0% (AUC = 0.952), increasing to 94.2% (AUC = 0.981) after limited classification-head adaptation on a separate subset. Together, these results identify load-dependent network flexibility and state-transition measures as candidate adjunctive biomarkers and define prospective multi-center validation as the next translational test.

item.title: A shared somatomotor structural substrate for motor function and behavioral symptoms in childhood and adolescence.
item.description:
Developmental cognitive neuroscience
Motor function and behavioral symptom dimensions frequently co-occur during childhood and adolescence, yet the neural architecture linking these domains has remained underspecified. The somatomotor system has been suggested as a candidate substrate, but whether the two domains converge on it, and whether such convergence resides in functional coupling or cortical structure, has not been characterized. Seventy-two typically developing children and adolescents (mean age 10.52 years, 50% female) completed postural assessment, structural MRI and resting-state fMRI, and caregiver-reported Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Association maps relating postural control and behavioral symptoms (three CBCL broadband composites) to functional connectivity and structural features were constructed independently, adjusted for age, sex, head motion, and body mass index, and their overlap within a prespecified sensorimotor set was tested with a permutation-based conjunction analysis. Postural control and behavioral symptoms converged on cortical folding of the left postcentral region: two shared features emerged against a chance expectation of 0.04 (permutation p = .0051). A composite of the shared features was associated with CBCL Total Problems (r = .43) and with postural sway (r = .39), related to symptoms as a general dimension rather than any single scale, and was independent of whole-brain functional connectivity. No connectivity measure was shared between the domains, and the direct motor-symptom association was non-significant. Motor function and behavioral symptom dimensions in childhood and adolescence converge on an early-established structural level of somatomotor organization rather than on its functional coupling. These findings position early-formed cortical folding of the somatomotor system as a candidate marker of general developmental liability, with implications for accessible motor measures as indicators of structurally anchored individual differences during development.

item.title: Principles of coarse-scale functional organization in occipitotemporal cortex.
item.description:
Communications biology
Occipitotemporal cortex (OTC) is known to support visual object processing, yet identifying general principles underlying its coarse-scale functional organization remains challenging. Previously proposed organizational dimensions, such as animacy or real-world size, may not generalize to more diverse, naturalistic stimuli and strong intercorrelations of object properties complicate determining which dimensions, if any, dominate OTC organization. We addressed these challenges through detailed analyses of the cortical topography underlying 15 object properties, using fMRI responses to thousands of natural images, focusing on animacy and size given their established prominence. Our results confirm many characteristics of the purported animacy-size organization, but reveal distinctions that challenge dominant notions of this organization, highlighting the importance of generalizing to large-scale naturalistic data. Beyond animacy and size, many properties could alternatively serve as organizational dimensions, yet none emerges as clearly dominant throughout OTC. Together, our findings reveal a more refined animacy-size organization than previously assumed and highlight challenges of assigning individual principles to account for OTC organization.

item.title: Creative cognition in frontotemporal dementia and brain health.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Creative cognition is central to human thought and is affected by brain disease. Recent findings by Altmayer and colleagues link creative impairment in frontotemporal dementia to rostral prefrontal functional differentiation. These findings motivate a framework for investigating network coordination, circuit physiology, experience-dependent plasticity, and bodily and social regulation in creativity and health.

item.title: The Separation-Distress Network as a Transdiagnostic Mechanism Linking Relational Adversity, Social Pain, and Psychopathology.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Relational trauma is a major contributor to the development of mental health disorders. This association likely reflects the social nature of humans and other mammals, whose survival depends on maintaining stable social bonds. When these bonds are threatened or disrupted, individuals experience social pain, a distress response mediated by the mammalian separation-distress network. During early development, this network is sensitive to maintaining proximity with caregivers, as independent survival is not yet possible. Converging evidence from ethology, psychodynamic and attachment theory, and social and affective neuroscience supports the function of this network. Because mammalian brains are inherently tuned to form social bonds, adverse relational experiences can disrupt socioemotional development and increase vulnerability to psychopathology. Neural substrates of separation distress include the anterior cingulate cortex, ventral septum, bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, dorsal preoptic area, dorsomedial thalamus, and periaqueductal gray, with endogenous opioids and glucocorticoids serving as key neurochemical modulators in the separation-distress response. Separation distress and adverse relational experiences also alter physiological systems implicated in psychopathology, including the HPA axis, autonomic nervous system activity, inflammation, and brain structure and connectivity. This paper argues that relational trauma and social pain are mediated by an evolutionarily conserved subcortical separation-distress network shared across predominantly mammalian species. Dysregulation of this network may represent one common mechanism underlying depression, social anxiety, suicidality, substance use disorders, borderline personality disorder, and other psychiatric conditions. Understanding the processes linking adverse relational experiences, separation-distress activation, and social pain may provide insights into the etiology and treatment of diverse disorders.

item.title: Expectation-driven gain modulation of preparatory spatial attention.
item.description:
eLife
The visual system can flexibly adjust attentional deployment to match task demands, but whether observers can proactively modulate the spatial scope of attention based on expectations about upcoming search difficulty remains unclear. According to the zoom lens model, attention can narrow or broaden its spatial extent, with narrower focus enhancing processing efficiency, a mechanism that would benefit target discrimination in crowded displays. We tested whether observers adjust attentional scope when expecting sparse versus dense search arrays by combining spatial cueing with block-wise manipulations of display density expectations. Participants performed a visual search task in which endogenous cues predicted target location, while blocks predominantly contained either sparse (1 target, 3 distractors) or dense (1 target, 7 distractors) displays. We applied inverted encoding models to broadband EEG data to reconstruct spatial channel tuning functions, enabling precise characterization of both the locus and breadth of attentional deployment. Behaviorally, expecting difficult searches selectively improved accuracy at cued locations without costs elsewhere. Consistent with this selective benefit, neural measurements revealed that expectancy enhanced the amplitude of spatially selective responses at the attended location but did not alter tuning width. These findings demonstrate that expectations about search difficulty modulate attention through gain-based signal enhancement rather than adjustments to spatial scope, revealing that preparatory attentional control operates via amplitude modulation within a stable spatial focus. This mechanism complements reactive attentional adjustments and provides an efficient means for the visual system to optimize processing under predictable task demands.

item.title: Learning rapidly reshapes brain microstructure: evidence from dense temporal sampling of diffusion MRI.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Learning is associated with rapid microstructural changes in the human brain, yet the precise temporal dynamics of these changes remain unclear. Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI) combined with task-based fMRI, we assessed microstructural changes throughout a declarative learning paradigm and subsequent rest. Seventy-four participants (36 females) learned image-location associations across four encoding-retrieval repetitions while undergoing interleaved functional and DW-MRI acquisitions. A matched control group (N=37, 21 females) underwent a similar imaging protocol without learning. Dense sampling of DW-MRI acquisitions (2146 images across 22 time points in 127 min) revealed that learning-induced mean diffusivity (MD) decreases emerged shortly after learning onset and continued to develop during post-learning rest. The most robust change was localized to the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus, a region also showing functional activation during encoding and retrieval. Linear mixed-effects modeling further confirmed a significant group-by-time interaction, with MD reductions in the left middle occipital/temporal gyrus emerging as early as ≈7 min after learning onset, becoming robust by ≈35-40 min, and persisting throughout the extended post-learning period, while controls showed no changes. Our findings demonstrate that learning-related microstructural plasticity unfolds continuously from encoding to offline consolidation, with learning-induced structural changes emerging in functionally engaged regions. Dense temporal sampling of DW-MRI offers a powerful approach to bridge functional activation and structural remodeling, providing evidence of when and where experience-dependent plasticity occurs during memory formation.Significance Statement How quickly does the brain's structure change when we learn? Using dense temporal sampling of diffusion-weighted MRI (DW-MRI; 2146 images) across more than 2 hours, we show that microstructural plasticity arises rapidly during learning and continues to develop during post-learning rest. These learning-induced changes are spatially precise and overlap with task-related functional activity. By capturing the entire progression of microstructural plasticity across the learning process, rather than just before and after a learning paradigm, our study provides insights into when and where learning-induced plasticity occurs, demonstrating that memory formation involves rapid, ongoing microstructural changes in functionally engaged regions.

item.title: Spatially localized fMRI metrics as predictive and highly distinct state-independent fingerprints.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Precision medicine and the investigation of brain-behavior associations require biomarkers that are stable (low intraindividual variability) and unique (high-interindividual variability) at the same time, hence calling them "fingerprints". The functional connectome (FC) has good "fingerprint properties", as individuals can be accurately identified in a database based on their FC. Importantly, research has shown lower intraindividual variability of more localized measures of brain function, such as regional homogeneity (ReHo) and (fractional) amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations ((f)ALFF), compared with the FC. Additionally, the predictiveness of behavior using the FC is modest at best. Here, with fMRI data from two publicly available datasets, we demonstrate that individuals can be identified with near-perfect accuracies using local functional fingerprints, especially the regional homogeneity (ReHo) fingerprint. Further analyses reveal that the dorsal attention network contributes most to the individual "uniqueness" of the ReHo fingerprint. Moreover, using a machine learning setup, we find that intraindividual variability of the ReHo fingerprint across sessions shows predictive signal for individual-level intelligence, albeit with model performance dependent on the condition. Last, using two other publicly available datasets, clinical applicability is demonstrated with high fingerprint accuracies and a significant correlation between fingerprint stability and intelligence in individuals with schizophrenia. Altogether, our findings suggest that the ReHo fingerprint is a good candidate for further exploration of applicability in precision medicine.

item.title: Cortical depth EEG-fMRI at 7T: Experimental setup and analysis pipeline to elucidate generating mechanisms of alpha oscillations.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Alpha band (8-13 Hz) electroencephalography (EEG) oscillations are central to cognition, but their generating mechanisms are poorly understood. Most laminar studies investigating origins of alpha oscillations rely on invasive animal intracranial recordings. To relate these findings to human alpha generation, non-invasive techniques need to be developed. Ultra-high-field (UHF, 7T) laminar functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) enables cortical depth resolved brain responses, and, combined with simultaneous EEG, offers new insight into human alpha generation mechanisms. This work presents a framework for studying the generating mechanisms of electrophysiological signals non-invasively in humans using simultaneous EEG laminar fMRI. Data were acquired on 10 participants during an eyes-closed/eyes-open paradigm. In 9 of 10 participants, the quality of EEG and Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were sufficient to observe a significant negative correlation between EEG alpha power and the BOLD signal in visual cortex grey matter. To improve depth specificity and mitigate pial-surface BOLD signal increases due to draining veins, we applied "deveining". The effects of each of the deveining analysis steps on the cortical depth profiles of the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were studied. The largest effect arose from excluding voxels in the tissue immediately surrounding veins. After deveining, the negative alpha-BOLD correlations were significantly weaker in the middle cortical depths than in superficial and deep depths. This depth dependence was absent when modelling the task with a boxcar regressor rather than EEG alpha power, suggesting specificity to spontaneous electrophysiological (alpha) fluctuations. In conclusion, we have established a method to non-invasively interrogate the origins of electrophysiological signals. Our alpha-BOLD depth profiles during the eyes-open/eyes-closed task (strongest correlations in superficial and deep layers) are consistent with activity in cortical depths typically associated with feedback/top-down processing, but we cannot definitively demonstrate causality from these data.

item.title: Respiratory phase orchestrates human olfactory cortical dynamics.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Olfaction is fundamental to perception, memory, and emotion, yet the neural basis of human odor processing remains poorly understood. We demonstrate that odor-evoked brain activity is organized by respiratory phase-not absolute time-revealing that natural breathing structures olfactory cortical dynamics. Using simultaneous nasal respiration and electroencephalography recordings in [Formula: see text] participants, we delivered naturalistic odors (peppermint, oregano, and grapefruit) synchronized to individual breathing cycles. Odor presentation elicited respiratory phase-locked event-related spectral perturbations (RPL-ERSPs) in frontal and temporal regions, emerging during the first breath after stimulus onset. The most discriminative neural signatures were theta-band activity during inhalation and alpha-band activity during exhalation, patterns that were obscured in traditional time-locked analyses due to natural variability in breath duration. Leave-one-subject-out cross-validation of RPL-ERSPs achieved reliable odor detection (peppermint: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.79; oregano: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.67; grapefruit: AUC [Formula: see text] 0.62), establishing that phase-locked features generalize across individuals. To connect neural responses to perceptual experience without relying on odor naming-which can be disproportionately impaired in some populations-we quantified odor recognition using free-response descriptions scored with a semantic-similarity approach. Behavioral recognition strength paralleled the neural decoding hierarchy across odors, establishing the perceptual validity of RPL-ERSPs. RPL-ERSPs revealed rapid habituation, with decoding performance declining over repeated presentations, due to selective degradation of the most informative phase-locked features. These findings establish respiratory rhythm as a temporal scaffold for human olfactory cortical processing, positioning RPL-ERSPs as a sensitive, task-free approach for assessing olfactory function. We provide an open-source, respiration-synchronized olfactometer design to enable replication and adoption.

item.title: Constructing events across perception, action, and thought.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
The brain organizes continuous experience into events that structure episodic memory and guide behavior. Traditional accounts have primarily focused on sensory discontinuities and prediction errors that trigger updates of event models. Here, we broaden this view to consider event boundaries arising during goal-directed behavior, spontaneous thought, and memory recall, including transitions generated in the absence of corresponding changes in sensory input. We propose that prediction error and uncertainty provide complementary signals for event model updating: prediction errors signal a violation of current expectations, whereas uncertainty may promote updating when upcoming states become difficult to predict. We further suggest that the hippocampus may serve as a candidate hub linking boundary-related representational changes across perception, action, and thought. Together, this framework offers an integrative account of how the brain detects and generates event structure in continuous experience to support memory and behavior.

item.title: Consumer neuroscience: the emerging science of everyday choices.
item.description:
Trends in cognitive sciences
Consumer neuroscience is a developing field at the intersection of neuroscience, psychology, economics, and marketing that seeks to uncover the neural and physiological mechanisms underlying consumer behavior. Building on early psychophysiological studies, the field has expanded substantially since the mid-2000s through an increasing range of methods and models. We highlight that its strength lies in spanning multiple levels of analysis to address marketing-relevant questions. We highlight four major trends driving the field: improving behavioral prediction, synthesizing evidence through multidataset analyses, developing formal models linking neural processes to consumer decision-making, and integrating brain and body measures. Together, these advances position consumer neuroscience as an integrative science with implications for marketing, policy, and consumer welfare.

item.title: Beyond scene construction: Mind time and the temporal organisation of cognition across hippocampal-cortical systems.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Scene-construction theory explains how spatially coherent event models support memory and imagination, although parts of their temporal organisation are less fully specified. Here we develop Mind Time as a theory of temporal organisation drawing on autobiographical memory and navigation to explain how events are related to one another and to a selected temporal origin across scales. Separating these represented relations from the operations that produce and revise them accommodates evidence for a distributed hippocampal-cortical system, including temporal judgements possible despite impaired episodic construction. Comparative findings constrain inferences about component capacities without resolving claims about subjective experience. The central theoretical proposal is that, during active construction, revising a temporal relation changes the information available to a represented self within the relevant history before a particular consequence is requested. An experiment would test whether this inferred state changes in advance and is available for use in subsequent imagination. Transpersonal extended Mental Time Travel (teMTT) extends this prediction to communication, through which a temporal revision should change another person's later reconstruction or planning. Together, Mind Time and teMTT specify how temporal relations constrain what a represented self can know or do, and how revising those relations changes subsequent reconstruction or planning.

item.title: Working memory supports cognitive control by orchestrating dimension-specific modulation during late conflict resolution.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Working memory plays a central role in cognitive control, yet how it shapes target- and distractor-related processing over time remains unclear. Here, we combined a working memory load manipulation with a modified Stroop task in which distractors preceded targets. Behaviorally, we found that pre-exposure to the distractor eliminated the congruency effect, but this benefit was absent under high load. This pattern suggests that the benefit of advance distractor presentation is sensitive to concurrent working-memory demands. Electrophysiologically, the distractor-locked lateralized readiness potential (LRP) indicated that working-memory load altered distractor-related response activation before target onset. After target onset, load-related modulation emerged during late conflict resolution, as indexed by the sustained potential (SP), whereas earlier intervals associated with attentional selection (posterior N2) and conflict monitoring (N450) did not show load-dependent modulation. Time-frequency decoding and representational similarity analysis further revealed distinct spectro-temporal profiles of target- and distractor-related processing: target-related coding emerged earlier in the theta band (540-780 ms), consistent with stimulus-response mapping, whereas distractor-related coding emerged later in the mu-beta band (870-1180 ms), consistent with response-related regulation. These findings highlight dimension- and stage-specific patterns of working-memory modulation during conflict resolution.

item.title: Repetition dissociates pointer and content-based representations in visual working memory: contrasting the CDA with multivariate shape decoding.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Memorizing a new phone number or address is hard at first, but becomes easier with repetition, as information shifts from working memory to long-term memory. Here we investigated how repetition affects the storage and transition of different aspects of mnemonic information by comparing univariate neural markers of active object storage with multivariate decoding of memory content. Thirty participants encoded lateralized stimuli from a continuous shape space into memory. Memory items were repeated six times in a row to induce learning. In line with earlier work, EEG recordings revealed that repetition led to a reduction in contralateral delay activity (CDA), a measure of active storage that has been taken to reflect a pointer-like representation of the individual object or its original source. In contrast, shape decoding during the retention and also after an impulse perturbation remained constant across repetitions. These results suggest that learning over repetitions reflects the abolishment of active and individuated object memory representations while passive, source-independent memory representations are retained.

item.title: Short-video experience and brain-state dynamics during the processing of rapidly changing video information in youth.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Background Short-video platforms frequently expose youth to rapidly changing video information. Processing such inputs requires large-scale brain networks to reorganize with the ongoing context. However, little is known about these dynamics or their association with prior short-video viewing experience. Methods A total of 108 youth aged 8-18 years completed resting-state and naturalistic movie-viewing fMRI scans. The movie comprised rapidly changing and relatively continuous segments. Hidden Markov models were applied to 17 cortical networks to identify recurrent brain states, and a joint rest-task analysis examined the context specificity of the main finding. Results Eight task-related brain states were identified. Five differed in fractional occupancy (FO) between conditions, and global switching was slightly higher during rapidly changing segments. State 7 was the only state showing an interaction with short-video viewing experience. Its FO was higher during relatively continuous than rapidly changing segments among participants reporting no prior Douyin use, whereas the condition difference was not significant among those reporting prior Douyin use. Visit frequency analyses showed a similar pattern. The interaction remained robust after covariate adjustment and was also observed in the joint rest-task analysis, with no significant group difference at rest. Conclusions Rapidly changing video information was associated with brain-state reorganization in youth. Douyin use was associated with lower State 7 occupancy during relatively continuous narrative segments; no significant group difference in the matched state's occupancy was detected at rest. These findings provide new evidence linking short-video viewing experience to context-dependent brain dynamics in youth.

item.title: Distinct neural representations of perceptual and numerical absence in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
The ability to represent absences is fundamental to human perception and cognition. Sensitivity to non-numerical absences depends on inferring a lack of sensory evidence, enabling the recognition of a lack of environmental resources or other objects. In turn, encoding numerical absence as a concept - in the form of the number zero - has enabled a multitude of technological and mathematical advances. Whether perceptual and conceptual absences rely on overlapping or distinct neural representations in the human brain, however, remains unknown. We employed three different tasks together with magnetoencephalography to characterise neural representations of absence evoked within perceptual and numerical domains. Using multivariate decoding and Bayes factor analyses, we replicate previous findings of shared representations of numerical absence across symbolic and non-symbolic formats. In contrast, we show that these representations of numerical absence are distinct from those evoked by non-numerical absences. This result held even after controlling for stimulus-level confounds which generate surface-level similarities between perceptual absences and non-symbolic empty sets. Our results extend a boundary between perception and cognition to the domain of absence and provide insight into the different mechanisms employed by the human brain to both perceive and conceive of absences.

item.title: Endogenous suspension of phenomenal consciousness during extended cessation: Regional homogeneity analysis of multi-participant 7T fMRI of an advanced meditative endpoint.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Extended cessation (EC) is a rare advanced meditative state characterized by the voluntary absence of reportable phenomenal experience, followed by reproducible aftereffects including immense mental clarity, equanimity, and peace. EC offers an endogenous model for investigating the mechanisms of consciousness. In a small-N case study (N = 3) using ultra-high-resolution 7T functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with dense within-subject sampling, we quantified whole-brain activity and related it to chemoarchitecture and cognitive maps. EC is marked by increased activity in unimodal sensory cortices and viscerosensory brainstem nuclei, and down-regulation in transmodal regions, subcortex and brainstem. Meta-analytic cognitive decoding linked EC to perceptual clarity and attentional processes, and away from distress-related domains. Multivariate coupling to normative neurotransmitter maps revealed that EC-related connectivity changes covaried with histaminergic H3 receptors topology. These findings constrain prevailing theories of consciousness by demonstrating that loss of experience need not entail global neural suppression, and supports accounts emphasizing selective precision modulation and hierarchical decoupling. More broadly, EC demonstrates that consciousness can cease without global suppression, suggesting a potential "reset" mechanism that fosters equanimity and the potential for flourishing.
